claims.text: The initial material is an SPS-fabricated W–Cu composite with tungsten particles embedded in a continuous copper matrix.
The initial SPS-fabricated W–Cu composite contains interfacial voids and phase separation.
Post-sintering pulsed near-infrared laser annealing will selectively reflow the copper phase.
Selective copper reflow will heal voids and improve wetting at W–Cu interfaces.
The intervention uses nanosecond near-infrared laser pulses with real-time temperature monitoring and feedback.
Temperature feedback can direct energy primarily to the copper phase without overheating the tungsten framework.
Processing is performed in argon at room pressure with nanosecond pulses calibrated to melt copper without boiling it.
Transient local melting enables capillary-driven flow of molten copper into interparticle voids and W–Cu interfacial gaps.
Rapid solidification after capillary infiltration consolidates the W–Cu interfaces.
Temperature feedback preserves the tungsten framework and avoids thermally induced stresses.
Laser annealing will significantly reduce porosity relative to untreated SPS W–Cu composites.
Improved interfacial bonding can improve mechanical properties in an SPS-fabricated composite.
Reduced porosity and improved W–Cu interfacial bonding will enhance thermal conductivity.
Laser-treated W–Cu will maintain or improve mechanical strength under fusion-relevant irradiation compared with untreated SPS W–Cu.
The intervention is intended for fusion-reactor-joint-scale components under controlled laboratory processing conditions.
Performance at larger scales or under varying irradiation flux remains unvalidated.
The magnitude of heat-transfer and mechanical-durability improvements, and the extent of scaling problems, are uncertain.
A controlled comparison of otherwise identical treated and untreated SPS W–Cu samples under simulated fusion irradiation can test the hypothesis.
Failure to reduce void fraction, increase thermal conductivity, and maintain or improve mechanical properties, or the appearance of new thermal-stress cracks, would falsify the hypothesis.
